2S00PsJ--U8.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 27 - Quranic Themes: Commands
2S00PsJ--U8.one_line: How to receive Quranic commands, explained through three: not allying with oppressors (60:1), caution with hostile family (64:14), and patience like Yunus lacked (68:48).
2S00PsJ--U8.summary: He opens with how a Muslim should hear the Quran's commands. A command is obligatory unless other evidence softens it, the call 'O you who believe' should make you stop and listen, and on Judgement Day the questions will mostly be about obedience to commands. Allah gains nothing from them, so every command serves us; even a harmful command would have to be obeyed, and Allah never asks for more than people could bear, such as all their wealth. The first command, 60:1, forbids taking Allah's enemies and your own as allies. It was needed because the companions leaned toward mercy, and it is needed now because leaders befriend those who openly want their people gone. Using the surah's later verses he limits it to those who fight your faith or drive you from your land, and applies it to Palestine: no alliance until everything is returned, a stance he calls basic decency rather than extremism, even if a proposed law brands it hate speech. The second, 64:14, says spouses and children can act as enemies; the answer is caution and a safe distance, never cutting family off, and pardon where possible. The third, 68:48, commands patience for Allah's decision without demanding to see the outcome, unlike Yunus who left his people too soon.

outline.heading: Opening
Commands as a major Quranic theme
outline.gist: Commands come addressed to believers, to humanity, to the Prophet and through earlier peoples; a Quranic command is obligatory unless evidence shows otherwise.

outline.heading: When a command is not an obligation
outline.gist: Only supplementary evidence in the verse, its context or the Prophet's explanation makes a command recommended, conditional or abrogated, so every command is taken seriously.

outline.heading: 'O you who believe': stop and listen
outline.gist: Commands are what we will be questioned about most: did you uphold justice, excellence, care of family as you were told?

outline.heading: Every command is in your interest
outline.gist: Allah gains nothing from obedience, so His commands protect and benefit us; even if a command were harmful it would still bind, so we have two reasons where one would do.

outline.heading: Allah never asks beyond what people can bear
outline.gist: Had He commanded self-harm, leaving homes or giving all wealth, most would refuse and their stinginess would surface; instead He asks 2.5% of idle wealth, which strengthens society.

outline.heading: 60:1: do not take My enemy and yours as allies
outline.gist: Some enemies are only personal; this verse concerns those who are enemies of both you and Allah, and he asks why such an obvious command was needed.

outline.heading: First reason: the companions' instinct to forgive
outline.gist: Islam had taught them to give the benefit of the doubt and work with everyone, so Allah had to draw a firm line for open enemies.

outline.heading: Second reason: leaders who cannot tell enemy from ally
outline.gist: The verse outlived its moment because today leaders ally with those who openly deny their people's right to exist; the verse will be held against them.

outline.heading: They expelled you for believing in Allah
outline.gist: If you migrated striving for Allah's pleasure, you cannot show love and support to those who drove out the Prophet and his followers.

outline.heading: 60:8-9: the limits of the prohibition
outline.gist: Allah allows kindness and justice toward disbelievers who did not fight your faith or expel you; only those who did, and those who aided them, are barred as allies, and one day Allah may put love between you.

outline.heading: Until the oppression stops
outline.gist: Until they stop persecuting belief and return what they took, no alliance or affection; Allah knows the love the companions hid in their hearts.

outline.heading: Palestine: no alliance until every millimetre returns
outline.gist: Not a political strategy but obedience: whatever it costs him, he will keep standing up and raise children who do the same until the land is returned and the oppression ends.

outline.heading: This is basic decency, not extremism
outline.gist: Refusing to befriend someone still oppressing you is normal human reasoning; as a child he wondered why the verse was needed, as an adult he saw people trusting those who openly plan to harm them.

outline.heading: When quoting the verse becomes hate speech
outline.gist: A proposed law could make this verse unquotable even for a descendant of Nazareth; a world run by whoever has the bigger bomb has no principles, but a Muslim stands by truth, wisely, whatever the cost.

outline.heading: Interlude
64:14: enemies among your spouses and children
outline.gist: This enmity is about competing interests, not politics; the response is not war but caution so they cannot take from you what you have built with Allah.

outline.heading: Keep a safe distance, never cut family off
outline.gist: You cannot ostracise or abandon family; no scenario of cutting off blood ends well, so keep caring and guiding while denying them the access to ruin you, and pardon if you can.

outline.heading: When the closest people turn against you
outline.gist: A Syrian proverb about spitting upward or downward and an old Arab poem of a man whose tribe killed his brother capture the bind: retaliation wounds yourself and forgiveness feels impossible.

outline.heading: Seek pardon tonight by pardoning family
outline.gist: Do not treat them as enemies even when they treat you so; on the 27th night, if you want Allah's pardon, pardon those of your blood.

outline.heading: 64:15-16: wealth and children are a test
outline.gist: Fear Allah as much as you can, listen and obey, and know that those saved from the greed of their own selves are the successful.

outline.heading: Interlude
Eid prayer belongs to the whole community
outline.gist: He will not hold a separate Eid in his own centre unless there is real need, because the sunnah is that Muslims pray Eid together rather than in half-empty separate gatherings.

outline.heading: 68:48: be patient for your Lord's decision
outline.gist: Al-Qalam has almost no practical command until its end, one of the first given to the Prophet: persevere until Allah decides; we do not choose when good prevails.

outline.heading: Make peace with not seeing the outcome
outline.gist: The Prophet died at sixty-three, only years before Islam reached three continents; we too will likely not see the results we work for.

outline.heading: Do not be like the companion of the whale
outline.gist: Yunus lost patience and left his people just before it mattered, then called out in distress from the whale; Allah's blessing rescued him, and the lesson is never to act in haste you will regret.

TFLNjnX55uI.one_line: The second half of the prayer: prostration as the closest point to Allah, a conversation rather than a list of demands, and endless reasons to seek forgiveness.
TFLNjnX55uI.summary: Continuing his nightly walk through the movements of the prayer, Sh. Adnan reaches its second half. Having stood, bowed and risen in praise, the worshipper is now allowed to move to three movements: two prostrations and the sitting between them. The Prophet told us to make much dua in prostration because it is likely to be answered, and that a servant is closest to his Lord while prostrating. Prostration is the most humble a person will ever be, a posture people never give to anyone but Allah. He asks people to treat it as a conversation with Allah, a response to the conversation Allah began through the Quran, not a list of demands with deadlines, and to learn the language of that conversation from the Prophet's duas and from the mother of Maryam speaking to her Lord at her daughter's birth. In the second reminder he explains that two prostrations give two chances to ask, and the sitting between them is for forgiveness of what has passed. The Prophet sought forgiveness a hundred times a day because his sensitivity was so high that any shortfall in his closeness to Allah warranted it, and we should seek forgiveness for not being our best, not only for sins.

eaTI4MgKJWQ.title: The Values of Islam: Love (al-Hubb) and Beauty (al-Jamal)
eaTI4MgKJWQ.one_line: Love and beauty are Islam's highest ideals, but they can only grow in a society that first secures justice, righteousness and core ethics.
eaTI4MgKJWQ.summary: Closing his series on the values of Islam, the sheikh presents love and beauty as high-order ideals that only make sense once a society has its core ethics in place. Ideals without the foundation become hollow, and young people sense the hypocrisy. He asks how love can exist where oppression reigns, using the verse that Allah may one day place love between believers and their enemies, which presupposes that the oppression ends first. He separates genuine love from selfish attachment that uses people for benefit, defining love as seeing another person as an extension of yourself. Because love makes a person vulnerable, it needs a just society to protect it, and he offers his own theory that all of Islam's ethics exist so that people can love safely. He traces love through the Quran and hadith, then turns to beauty: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, yet beautifying houses, masjids or cities is pointless when the interior is full of injustice. He ends with Ali grieving over Talhah in the middle of a battle, and with the early Muslims, who had little wealth but carried the faith across the world because they loved. He asks the community to secure the basics so love and beauty can flourish.

outline.gist: A perfect house without love is pointless; Allah asks for adornment at the masjid and beautiful recitation, but beauty must sit on substance.

outline.gist: The highest people in Jannah want nothing but their appointments to see Allah's face, the source of all beauty.

outline.gist: Without righteousness and justice we lose the ability to love genuinely and appreciate beauty, and life becomes dull.

outline.gist: Love is felt even in food and small gestures; in Ramadan we are waiting for a moment of loving Allah and feeling His love.

outline.heading: No lasting love or beauty without the basics
outline.gist: Without the core values the experience is artificial; with them every leaf and star becomes a sign of Allah's beauty.

outline.heading: If family and wealth are dearer than Allah (9:24)
outline.gist: Putting anything above love of Allah and His Messenger means missing the most important thing.

outline.heading: Early Muslims: simple means, deep love
outline.gist: They had plain masjids but felt and expressed love and beauty, and kept their love even through bitter disagreements.

outline.heading: Ali and Talhah at the battle
outline.gist: Ali weeps over the dying Talhah, hopes they will be brothers in Jannah with rancour removed, and buries him, though they fought on opposite sides.

outline.heading: A loveless community and a loveless marriage
outline.gist: Without love people tire of their faith and relationships; a marriage needs justice and fair treatment before love can grow.

outline.heading: Series recap: the society Islam aims for
outline.gist: Forgiveness, chivalry, generosity, love and beauty grow from protected basics; the Sahaba carried the faith out of love for the Prophet.

xMqwsBv8UB4.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 27: Seventh Night of Tahajjud
xMqwsBv8UB4.one_line: On the 27th night: ask Allah for pardon that erases sins completely, and earn it by pardoning those who wronged you.
xMqwsBv8UB4.summary: The 27th night reminders are both about pardon. In the first he says the night is about your own ability to pardon others: the Prophet taught Aisha to ask Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon on this night, and the verse revealed about Abu Bakr asks believers to pardon and overlook if they want Allah to forgive them. He cites the words found on the Prophet's sword, give to whoever deprives you, reconnect with whoever cuts you off, pardon whoever wrongs you and be good to whoever harms you, as the code the Prophet lived by, and Umar's public release of everyone from any claim he had on them, reasoning that Allah will not be outdone by His servants. In the second reminder he separates forgiveness from pardon: a forgiven sin stays in your book, stamped forgiven, while a pardoned sin is gone as if it never happened. He paints a scene of searching your book on the Day of Judgement for a sin you feared and never finding it, because Allah erased it from the record, from the angels and from everyone who saw it. He asks people to spend the coming minutes finding the strength to pardon someone, because it is impossible to pardon and not be pardoned.

outline.gist: An imagined scene: you flip through your book for the date of a sin you feared, cannot find it, ask the person involved and the recording angels, and it never comes up before Allah.

outline.heading: Allah erases it from every memory
outline.gist: Allah tells you that on the 27th night of Ramadan 2026 you asked for pardon and He erased the sin from your book and from the memory of the angels, witnesses and those affected; soon you forget it too.

outline.heading: Someone here has to pardon
outline.gist: He needs at least one person in the room to find the strength to pardon someone who wronged or oppressed them, however hard it is.

outline.heading: You cannot outdo Allah in generosity
outline.gist: Use the coming minutes to forgive those who wronged you: it is impossible to pardon and not be pardoned, and forgiving lifts a burden off you.

94sXD9O24Ys.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 29 - Quranic Themes: Outcomes
94sXD9O24Ys.one_line: Every choice has an outcome: ethical consistency in al-Balad, the path of ease in al-Layl, and the two final destinations in al-Bayyinah.
94sXD9O24Ys.summary: On the last night of the series he takes outcomes as a Quranic theme: every choice leads somewhere, and the Quran insists we own our choices in a world where the rich and connected escape consequences. The end of Ramadan raises the same question as the end of life, and returning to how you were before wastes a month that was meant as a workshop and launching pad. From al-Balad he draws ethical consistency: the steep path is freeing captives and feeding the hungry on a day you yourself are hungry, because a value that disappears in hard times is only a preference. The Prophet, expelled from his own city, never became cruel. Believers keep each other steady by urging patience and compassion, and only two outcomes exist. From al-Layl he explains that givers and the God-conscious are eased toward ease in this life itself, inner ease rather than freedom from hardship, while the stingy are eased toward hardship, so the deal is win-win or lose-lose. Al-Bayyinah names the worst and best of creation by their choices, made against relentless time. The best are with their Lord; mutual satisfaction, seeing Allah's face and the healing of every inner wound await those who revere Him.

outline.heading: Opening
A guest who leaves too quickly
outline.gist: No one knows if they will see another Ramadan; he measures his own life by which Ramadans events fell between, so cherish its final hours.

outline.heading: Outcomes as a Quranic theme
outline.gist: Every choice and path ends in an outcome you are stuck with; the Quran's insistence on owning consequences is refreshing where the rich and connected get bailed out.

outline.heading: What is the outcome of your Ramadan?
outline.gist: The end of the month, of a recitation of the Quran and of a life all ask what comes next; slipping back to how things were wastes thirty days of momentum.

outline.heading: Ramadan is the workshop, not the outcome
outline.gist: Ramadan is where you push and strive so that the outcome, in a long life or after death, is good.

90:11-16: the steep path of ethical consistency
outline.gist: Free the captive and feed an orphan relative or a destitute person on a day you are hungry yourself: generosity that stops when times are hard was never a value.

outline.heading: A value is always there
outline.gist: Rich or poor, a real ethic defines your character; al-Balad came as the Prophet was being driven from the city of his forefathers back to Ibrahim.

outline.heading: Expelled but never embittered
outline.gist: Being driven from his city did not make the Prophet cruel, rude or hateful; he had climbed that obstacle long before and stayed who he was meant to be.

outline.heading: 90:17-18: urging patience and compassion
outline.gist: Believers remind each other when one loses perseverance or grows harsh; that mutual advice keeps the values alive and puts them among the people of the right.

outline.heading: 90:19-20: the people of the ill omen
outline.gist: Those who rejected the signs, who called prophets a bad omen, face a fire closed over them; there are only two outcomes and no third way.

outline.heading: Keep advising one another
outline.gist: Without mutual reminders to patience and compassion we lose our principles, then the deen, and then all sense of right and wrong.

outline.heading: 92:4-7: diverse paths, one common core
outline.gist: Everyone's striving differs, and that is fine, but all must share giving, God-consciousness and affirming the best that was revealed.

outline.heading: Eased toward ease or toward hardship
outline.gist: Al-yusra here is a way of life, Islam itself, not only Paradise; the stingy and self-sufficient are eased toward the hardest life.

outline.heading: Win-win or lose-lose
outline.gist: Had Allah offered a bad life now for Paradise later, people would weigh the trade; instead the right choice brings ease now and the best outcome later.

outline.heading: Ease is inside the heart
outline.gist: Not freedom from illness or poverty, but inner ease; wealth and health mean nothing without love, a good family and sleep with a clear conscience.

outline.heading: Interlude
Follow Muhammad and find ease
outline.gist: He addresses the young: Islam is the best way to live; ask those who lived with Allah whether they found it hard.

outline.heading: Companions who left with nothing, content
outline.gist: Many died with no inheritance yet fully satisfied; even a few nights of Ramadan gave you a taste of that inner peace.

outline.heading: Fasting to feed the spirit
outline.gist: Set the body aside for a month and nurture the spirit, and you find something that outweighs life's sorrow; the Quran recited all month is that ease.

outline.heading: 98:6: the worst of creatures by their own choice
outline.gist: Disbelievers among the People of the Book and the pagans are called the worst of creation because they had a choice that could have led elsewhere.

outline.heading: Time has no mercy
outline.gist: You hold your destiny; preoccupation with legacy and wealth leaves no time for what comes next, and time marches on without pause, so decide now.

outline.heading: 98:7-8: 'with their Lord' is enough
outline.gist: The best of creation made hard right choices; his teacher said the words 'with their Lord' suffice, everything after is an extra.

outline.heading: Rivers flowing beneath: self-sufficient gardens
outline.gist: Land watered from someone else's territory lives in fear of a dam upstream; Paradise's rivers run beneath its gardens so nothing can be cut off.

outline.heading: Mutual satisfaction

tlseapPw7MQ.title: The Values of Islam: Nobility and Generosity (Muru'ah and Karam)
tlseapPw7MQ.one_line: Muru'ah, the fulfilment of one's humanity, and generosity are high ideals Muslims must revive once the basic ethics are secure.
tlseapPw7MQ.summary: Continuing the week of high ideals, he stresses that values such as forgiveness, nobility and generosity are not obligations one is punished for neglecting, but they flourish only where the non-negotiable basics of justice and righteousness are secure. He explains muru'ah, rooted in the Arabic word for a human being, as reaching the full potential of humanity: doing whatever adorns character and avoiding whatever dents it. Pre-Islamic Arabs prized it, competing to be the one who says 'leave it to me' when someone is in need, and Islam simply purified the intention. Khadijah's description of the Prophet carrying the burdens of others shows he lived this before and after revelation, and hadith critics would reject a narrator whose conduct lacked muru'ah even if nothing he did was unlawful. His favourite story is of Uthman ibn Talhah, not yet Muslim, escorting Umm Salamah hundreds of kilometres to Madinah with complete propriety and never mentioning it. On generosity he contrasts Hatim's fame with the Prophet's generosity and Abu Bakr's giving away all he had, ending with a story of Abu Bakr giving even his clothes to the poor. He calls for these ideals to be revived in homes and in raising children.

outline.heading: Beyond zakat: a generous society
outline.gist: Zakat is the obligation, but the ideal is a society that enjoys giving, which injustice makes impossible.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr gives away his caravan and his clothes
outline.gist: Finding Madinah in need, he gave away a whole caravan and then his clothing, arriving at the Prophet's gathering in a wheat sack.

outline.heading: Is he pleased with his Lord?
outline.gist: He was told Allah was pleased with him and asked if he was pleased with his Lord, and wept; he later regained wealth.

outline.heading: Bring these ideals back home
outline.gist: Children must be raised to be generous and noble, or Muslims will remain far from what they once were.

uexim-XLSTw.speaker_note: sixth episode of his own series at Muslim Wellness Network; refers to his own Tazkiyah series and to his children; brief audience Q&A at the end
uexim-XLSTw.title: The Philosophy of Islamic Thought #6: Psychology, Physical Health and the Lifestyle of Wellness in Islam
uexim-XLSTw.one_line: Islam's layered model of the human self, its ethic of the body as a trust, and a balanced lifestyle, with cautions on jinn, magic and mental illness.
uexim-XLSTw.summary: He opens by explaining that young Muslims doing dawah must argue from root principles, such as a theory of human nature, rather than from isolated stories, and that faith should never be built on or lost over tertiary narrations. Islam sees the human being as layered: body, spirit, soul, intellect, conscience and subconscious, each named in the Quran, so it offers a real psychological model rather than mystical poetry. The subconscious absorbs everything poured into it, so garbage in means garbage out. Humans are morally responsible, mind, body and spirit affect one another, and discipline can reshape character. Tazkiyah is a third of the din. Human nature cannot be changed, only behaviour, which explains rules on seclusion and safeguarding property; Islam embraces nature and channels it rather than repressing it. The nafs is a loving but ignorant cheerleader that can be tamed in stages, while Shaytan is weak but unpersuadable. The body is a trust: no self-harm, no excess or ascetic neglect, value strength and eat lightly. A well lifestyle has prayer as a structured pause, moderate eating, disciplined sleep, community and service. He firmly rejects jinn possession and present-day black magic as explanations for illness, insists ruqya never replaces professional care, and says mental illness is not a sign of weak iman.

outline.heading: Why this series: dawah at the ideological level
outline.gist: Non-Muslims steeped in other philosophies ask what Islam's theory of knowledge, ethics and economics are, and Muslims must answer at that level.

outline.heading: Young Muslims will be sized up by ideologues
outline.gist: Older believers may not need this, but students facing atheists, liberals or Marxists must explain the principles behind the examples.

outline.heading: Argue from root principles, not end rulings
outline.gist: On modesty or polygamy, ask what in the moral system or view of human nature someone actually disputes.

outline.heading: Do not build or lose faith on tertiary stories
outline.gist: A narration in Bukhari should not shake your iman; faith rests on the big framework questions, not on doubt websites.

outline.heading: The architecture of the self: the atheist view
outline.gist: Materialism sees a person as the sum of evolution, synapses and environment with no further layer.

outline.heading: Not a mind trapped in a disposable body
outline.gist: The mind can imagine what the body never can, as with Star Wars, but Islam sees a layered creature rather than a floating mind.

outline.heading: The layers named: body, spirit, soul, intellect, conscience, subconscious
outline.gist: The Quran distinguishes them clearly; modern psychology also speaks of a self beyond the ego, and Allah breathing His spirit into us signals an intimate bond.

outline.heading: When one layer is sick: the heart and the subconscious
outline.gist: Everything seen, heard and suffered pours into the subconscious; feed it haram and you get haram out.

outline.heading: A psychological model, not mystical poetry
outline.gist: Islam's model parallels exposure in modern psychology and deserves recognition as a competing, often superior model.

outline.heading: Assumption one: humans are morally responsible
outline.gist: We do not prosecute a pet lion; Western thought wants moral responsibility without the metaphysics that generates it.

outline.heading: Assumption two: mind, body and spirit affect each other
outline.gist: Accountability requires mental soundness and functioning senses, which is why the born deaf-blind are not held accountable.

outline.heading: Assumption three: discipline and reflection reshape character
outline.gist: How you are need not be how you stay; the model is closer to virtue ethics than reductionist neurochemistry, without denying biology.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah as a third of the din
outline.gist: Practice, belief and inner purification; morality fails without constant self-questioning about motives like vanity, anger or selfishness.

outline.heading: Taking the best of revelation and the mystery of the spirit
outline.gist: Self-purification lets you use texts in their best way; the spirit remains a matter of Allah's command.

outline.heading: Human nature cannot change, behaviour can
outline.gist: Men are men and women have natures too; two people left on an island will pair up, so Islam regulates behaviour such as seclusion.

outline.heading: Unattended wealth teaches theft
outline.gist: A Syrian proverb and the requirement that stolen property was properly secured both acknowledge human nature.

outline.heading: Islam embraces human nature rather than repressing it
outline.gist: No shame in what you feel; desires are expressed through healthy, regulated channels, and vows of celibacy are not accepted.

outline.heading: The nafs: your loving but ignorant cheerleader
outline.gist: Born where spirit met body, it wants survival, food, mating and dominance; not evil, it can be taught over time.

outline.heading: Shaytan: weaker but unpersuadable
outline.gist: Unlike the nafs he cannot be influenced, but he has little real power.

outline.heading: Stages of taming the nafs and the thought-action-emotion cycle
outline.gist: From submission to struggle, coercion, acceptance and love; changing thoughts and actions eventually changes feelings.

outline.heading: Modern therapy echoes the Prophetic model
outline.gist: A psychiatrist tells a depressed patient to wake, dress and walk daily; behaviour change reshapes the mind.

outline.heading: The body as a trust: five principles
outline.gist: No self-harm, no excess in activity or idleness, strength is valued, prevention beats cure and overconsumption is discouraged.

outline.heading: Against ascetic neglect of the body
outline.gist: Early ascetics starved themselves; Ali drank cold water because it draws deeper gratitude.

outline.heading: Fasting as metabolic discipline
outline.gist: The body is entrusted, so no tattoos or mutilation; Ramadan recalibrates appetite and metabolism rather than starving.

outline.heading: Prayer as embodied devotion and hygiene as faith
outline.gist: Each posture carries a spiritual meaning, and cleanliness is part of the din itself.

outline.heading: The least followed hadith: the stomach
outline.gist: No vessel is worse to fill than the stomach; leave a third for breath, consume less so you are healthier and the planet suffers less.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: write down your schedule
outline.gist: When someone cannot memorize Quran he has them write and stare at their day; moderation is the principle.

outline.heading: Spiritual rhythm: prayer as a structured pause
outline.gist: Each prayer is a time-out that resets you amid the day's stimuli and leads to better decisions.

outline.heading: Nutritional moderation
outline.gist: Overconsumption is corrosive physically and spiritually; enjoy meals but be reasonable.

outline.heading: Sleep discipline
outline.gist: The Prophet never stayed up a full night outside battle; eating more makes you sleep more, and students should be asleep before midnight on weekdays.

outline.heading: Afiyah: wellbeing of body, mind and spirit
outline.gist: Wellbeing is the best gift; maintain it in every dimension.

outline.heading: Community health: isolation is spiritually risky
outline.gist: Solitude for reflection is good but loneliness is not; congregational worship and visiting the sick keep people connected.

outline.heading: Service heals
outline.gist: Studies now confirm altruism improves wellbeing; healing another suffering soul heals your own.

outline.heading: The feedback loop and why balance is harder than extremism
outline.gist: Sin disturbs the heart, which unsettles the psyche, the body and spiritual discipline; break the cycle anywhere and keep calibrating.

outline.heading: Jinn cannot hijack the psyche
outline.gist: Exorcisms are baseless and harmful; telling a paranoid patient a jinn is inside him plants a belief no medication can remove.

outline.heading: Black magic as superstition today
outline.gist: Marital breakdowns come from ego and incompatibility, not a paper hidden with goat hair.

outline.heading: Envy and the evil eye are real but not a diagnosis
outline.gist: Take the protective steps, but look for real causes so you can change outcomes.

outline.heading: Tailored rulings for OCD, anxiety and depression
outline.gist: People with mental illness need personal guidance, and some tazkiyah practices like humility talks can harm the self-loathing.

outline.heading: Ruqya is not a substitute for care
outline.gist: Recite over loved ones daily, but just as ruqya does not set a fracture, it does not replace professional treatment.

outline.heading: Mental illness is not weak iman
outline.gist: Blaming weak faith deprives people of simple treatment; strong iman helps manage illness but does not replace care.

outline.heading: Wellness as Islam in action
outline.gist: Values become concrete in how the Prophet slept, ate, walked and spoke.

outline.heading: Q&A: stages or departments of the nafs
outline.gist: The nafs commanding evil is the same self being tamed; the more connected the conscience is to Allah, the more it reproaches the self.
